name: Omex CivServ Synth-Standard Service Uniform
description: Slate-grey polyweave tunic and tapered trouser set cut for extended-limb proportions, with accordion-fold panels at every joint to accommodate non-human articulation. Omex corporate teal piping runs the seams, and a magnetic chest panel displays the unit's service designation. Maintenance panels at the shoulder and hip allow quick chassis access without full undress. Fabric is stain-resistant and rated for daily industrial laundering.
functionality: Accordion joint panels, magnetic ID chest display, hip and shoulder maintenance access ports.
what_it_says: This unit is owned, assigned, and expected to be invisible while working.
story_hooks: The unit has sewn a single unauthorized stitch — a tiny red thread — inside the left cuff where no scanner looks.
The service designation panel has been swapped with a deceased unit's ID; someone is hiding in plain sight.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian two-piece uniform with a distinctly non-human silhouette. The tunic falls straight from shoulders with subtle tapering at the torso, while the trousers follow an extended proportional cut. Accordion pleats at elbows, knees, and hip joints create a segmented, almost biomechanical appearance. The overall effect reads as corporate-sanctioned synthetic labor wear—clinical, modular, designed for function over form.
physical_description.fit: Precisely tailored for augmented physiology. Relaxed through the torso with compression zones at the torso. Trousers cut narrow through thigh but with intentional slack at knee and ankle joints to allow accordion folds to expand. Sleeves feature similar joint articulation. The fit prioritizes mobility over human proportions.
physical_description.primary_material: Slate-grey polyweave composite—synthetic blend rated for industrial durability and repeated chemical cleaning. Slightly lustrous finish suggests polymer coating for stain resistance.
physical_description.texture: Smooth, almost plastic-like surface with subtle ribbing along the accordion fold lines. When the joints flex, the fabric creates visible creases that are engineered rather than accidental. Feels synthetic and slightly cool to touch.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant slate grey (cool, neutral, corporate) with bright teal piping running all major seams and edges. Teal creates visual segmentation, emphasizing the modular construction. No patterns—pure utilitarian color blocking.
physical_description.closures: Magnetic snap system across the chest panel (displays service designation). Side-seam friction-fit closures on trousers. Shoulder and hip maintenance panels feature quick-release toggle clasps for rapid chassis access.
distinctive_features: Accordion-fold flex panels at all major joints (elbows, knees, hips, shoulders, neck)
Magnetic chest display panel with service designation slot
Quick-access maintenance hatches at shoulder and hip
Omex corporate teal piping as brand identifier and functional seam markers
Reinforced stress points at joint articulations
Tapered cut suggesting extended-limb or synthetic body proportions
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 corporate service wear. Signals formal employment by a mid-tier corp (Omex), not street-level but not executive luxury. The synthetic nature and modular design mark the wearer as likely augmented or non-human.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this identifies the wearer as corporate service labor—maintenance, logistics, or operational support role within Omex's GLMZ operations. The design's non-human accommodation suggests the wearer is synthetic, heavily augmented, or an autonomous unit in human-facing roles. A badge of regulated employment in the corpo hierarchy.
physical_description.condition_typical: Pristine to well-maintained. The stain-resistant coating means daily industrial laundering leaves it looking factory-fresh. Any wear would be localized to flex points (accordion creases becoming more pronounced, piping slightly dulled from repeated flexion). Rarely patched—easier to replace than repair.
